extracted.intended_audience: media scholars, communication researchers, news editors, and journalists interested in foreign-news selection
extracted.subtask_description: A framework for evaluating why particular foreign events are selected as news, enumerating structural, identification, sensation, and ideological determinants and showing how ideology explains comparative coverage differences. Useful for researchers and editors benchmarking selection biases and designing homepage/newsroom selection models.

rubrics_metrics.name: Magnitude of Event
rubrics_metrics.description: Number of people affected, severity of impact (Galtung & Ruge threshold).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Larger-scale events that affect many people or have severe consequences pass the Galtung & Ruge magnitude threshold and therefore have higher news value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proximity
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Events closer in physical distance or cultural similarity to the home audience are more likely to be selected; proximity includes both geographic and cultural dimensions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Power Position
rubrics_metrics.description: Eliteness of nations and persons involved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Events involving powerful states, elite actors, or high-status institutions carry greater news value because of their perceived significance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Predictability (Schedulability)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Events that fit the timing and scheduling needs of newsrooms (e.g., anticipated events, anniversaries) are more likely to be covered because they can be planned into editorial cycles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultural Affinity
rubrics_metrics.description: Similarity of foreign actors to domestic readers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Audiences identify more with actors who share cultural traits; affinity increases perceived relevance and thus selection probability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Linguistic Compatibility
rubrics_metrics.description: English-language sources preferred globally; native-language sources preferred locally.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Availability of reporting in languages accessible to the newsroom/audience raises coverage likelihood; language compatibility shapes source choice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Familiar-Type Events
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Events that match well-known story templates (e.g., coups, elections, natural disasters) are easier to process editorially and resonate with audiences, increasing selection chances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Drama
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stories with dramatic stakes and unresolved outcomes attract audience attention and are prioritized (audience-pull factor).

rubrics_metrics.name: Conflict
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conflictual events—armed clashes, wars, major disputes—have strong news value due to their inherent newsworthiness and audience interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Negativity
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Negative events (disasters, failures, crimes) are preferentially selected because they draw and retain audience attention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cold War Bloc Coverage Asymmetry
rubrics_metrics.description: Pre-1989 Western media systematically over-covered Eastern bloc instability and under-covered Western bloc instability of comparable magnitude.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical example illustrating that ideological alignment (Cold War blocs) produced systematic asymmetries in coverage independent of event magnitude or other structural news values.

rubrics_metrics.name: Friend-vs-Enemy Framing
rubrics_metrics.description: Same event categorized differently depending on which side the actor was on (a coup becomes 'liberation' or 'putsch' depending on alignment).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Framing depends on perceived alignment; editorial language and categorization will vary to present allied actors positively and adversaries negatively, affecting selection and presentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Civilizational Privileging
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories from 'our' civilization (Western Europe, North America) carry more news value than equally important stories from 'other' civilizations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors and audiences privilege events within their civilizational frame, producing systematic coverage biases against regions seen as 'other.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Implicit National Interest Hooks
rubrics_metrics.description: Foreign stories preferred when they bear on the home country's foreign-policy priorities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Relevance to national strategic or policy interests increases a foreign story's newsworthiness; proximity in interest, not just geography, matters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Source-Country Media-System Bias
rubrics_metrics.description: Coverage flows along ideological lines via international news agencies; the agency's worldview leaks into source selection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Selection is affected by which international news agencies and source countries dominate feed; these sources carry ideological biases that shape what events are available and emphasized.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ideology as a Fourth Dimension
rubrics_metrics.description: Ideological orientation — the implicit world-political map of editors and audiences — is a major and irreducible determinant of foreign-news selection alongside structural (importance), supply, and audience-pull factors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Models of newsworthiness should include ideology explicitly; ignoring ideology leads to systematic misclassification of selection causes and predictive failures around comparative coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparative-Coverage Method: Fixed Event-List Benchmarking
rubrics_metrics.description: Compare multiple countries' media coverage against a fixed event-list to detect selection variance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Westerståhl & Johansson's method: hold event universe constant, control for Galtung-Ruge factors, and measure how ideological alignment explains residual variance; this is a recommended empirical approach for testing ideological asymmetries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Operationalizability: Benchmark and Test for Ideological Asymmetries
rubrics_metrics.description: Story selection can be benchmarked against a global event list and tested for ideological asymmetries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical implication for newsroom models and homepage algorithms: construct a global event benchmark and measure deviations in coverage patterns to reveal ideological biases; useful for auditing and improving selection fairness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Predictive Implication: Coverage Gap Prediction
rubrics_metrics.description: The model predicts systematic comparative coverage gaps (e.g., lower coverage of African coups vs. European political instability).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the ideology+news-values model to anticipate which regions/events will be under- or over-covered relative to structural expectations, informing editorial corrective actions or algorithmic adjustments.
